To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the OH Meinel band emission intensities show a maximum in September and minimum during December, while the O*2 emission intensities are maximum during September and minimum during January.
the equivalent energy loss rates by the OH and O2 emissions are 0.39 and 0.12, respectively, during the period December/January and 0.98 and 0.23, respectively, during September.

the equivalent energy loss rates by the OH* and O*2 radiations show a seasonal variation with maximum values during September (0.98 and 0.2 K/day*, respectively) and minimum values during December/January.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the mesospheric energy losses through the radiations of OH and O2 atmospheric bands at Cachoeiras Paulista (23.2° S, 44.9° W), Brazil.
the study of the mesospheric energy balance through the radiations emitted by the vibrationally excited hydroxyl radical and the electronically excited molecular oxygen.
the study of the mesospheric energy budget by the OH* and O*2 emissions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the total energy loss rates due to OH and O2 radiations are 0.51 and 1.2 K/day* during December/January and September, respectively.
the OH* Meiner bands dominate the total energy loss rate in the mesosphere.
the energy loss rates by the OH* and O*2 radiations are not constant, but they are variable during the year.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the energy loss rates by the OH and O2 emissions are in good agreement with the energy input rates from the solar radiation, suggesting that these emissions play a major role in the energy balance of the nighttime mesosphere.
the energy loss rates by the OH* and O2 radiations at 23° S are of the same order of magnitude and are in good agreement with the values reported for the northern hemisphere.

the equivalent energy loss rates by the OH* and O*2 radiations are 0.50 K/day and 0.25 K/day, respectively, for the period from October to December 1989 and 1.20 K/day and 1.00 K/day, respectively during the period from January to December 1999.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the energy loss rate by O2 radiation is about 30% of the energy loss rate of OH radiation.
the OH* Meiel bands are the main contributor to the total energy loss rate, with the O*2 emission playing a secondary role.
the equivalent energy loss rate is higher during the summer months than in winter months.
